tasks.short: Look at the client's skin or hair, check past products and reactions, recommend and explain products, and give aftercare instructions.

steps.what: Hairdresser looks at the client's skin or hair and asks about routines and reactions
Hairdresser looks up earlier products and noted allergies on the paper client card
Hairdresser recommends cosmetics, lotions and creams and explains their use
Hairdresser writes product names and how to use them on a card for the client
Client decides and buys products at the counter
Hairdresser notes the products sold on the client card

tasks.design: The digital client card in the salon system ({OTHER}) shows earlier treatments, products bought and recorded reactions at the chair, and checkout writes products sold to the card. The hairdresser picks the matching aftercare sheets, which the system sends to the client after the visit; the advice itself stays a conversation.
tasks.previous_blocker: Client history sat on paper cards, and aftercare instructions were handwritten.
tasks.enabler_now: Salon systems keep paperless client cards with treatment and purchase history, intake forms and messages.
tasks.still_hard: Notes on skin conditions or dye reactions are health data and need explicit consent; advice depends on seeing and touching.
tasks.human_edge: Reading a client's skin and habits and recommending what they will actually use.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; history is at hand and instructions are sent.

reach.task: Recommend a home routine after a facial
reach.learn: Whether sent aftercare sheets raise repeat product purchases.

evidence.claim: A Dutch salon system keeps paperless client cards with treatment and purchase history, notes, photos and signed intake forms.
Notes on skin conditions, allergies or dye reactions are health data; outside a healthcare contract they usually need explicit consent.
The business keeps its administration and receipts for seven years.

assumptions: Boundary: from looking at the client to the sale recorded; the treatment itself is outside.

Input contract: products sold written to the card by checkout; reactions and allergies recorded by the hairdresser with explicit consent on a signed intake form; aftercare sheets kept by the salon owner; fallback is the paper card.
Client time is outside the hairdresser's savings.
Assessment and advice do not change.
unknowns: Whether the salon already uses a salon system.
Share of clients who buy products.
research_questions: Do sent aftercare sheets raise repeat product purchases?

incremental.description: Hairdresser asks consent and records reactions on the intake form.
Salon owner keeps aftercare sheets current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Salons where few clients buy products, or that already keep digital cards, save little.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Demonstrate techniques, watch and correct assistants, plan who does which client, track mastered techniques and give feedback.

steps.what: Senior stylist demonstrates cutting and colour techniques to assistants
Senior stylist watches assistants and other hairdressers work and corrects them
Senior stylist notes which techniques each assistant has mastered in a notebook
Senior stylist plans who does which client and training slots in the paper agenda
Senior stylist gives feedback talks to assistants

tasks.design: The salon system's online agenda ({OTHER}) holds each staff member's services, so assistants can only be booked for treatments they are signed off for, and training slots sit in the same agenda. A short skill checklist per assistant is kept in a shared document in {DOCS}; demonstrating, watching and feedback stay in person.
tasks.previous_blocker: Planning and skill tracking lived in a paper agenda and a notebook.
tasks.enabler_now: Salon booking systems hold staff calendars and services per staff member.
tasks.still_hard: Teaching is hands-on, and a skill list is only as good as the senior's judgement.
tasks.human_edge: Showing an assistant the feel of a technique and knowing when they are ready for a paying client.
tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; planning and tracking are quicker.

reach.task: Plan staff and training across the week
reach.learn: Whether services per staff member reduce mis-booked treatments.

evidence.claim: A Dutch salon system offers an online agenda with staff calendars, online booking and reminders.
A works council is required from 50 staff; smaller salons have no consent step for agenda systems.

assumptions: Boundary: from demonstration to feedback; formal apprenticeship assessments are outside.
Input contract: services per staff member set by the salon owner from the skill checklist kept by the senior stylist; fallback is the paper agenda.
Assistant practice time is outside the stylist's savings.
Teaching, supervision and feedback do not change.
unknowns: Whether the salon uses an online agenda.
research_questions: Do mis-booked treatments for assistants fall when services follow the skill list?

incremental.description: Senior stylist keeps the skill checklist and services per assistant current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Small salons with one assistant plan and track by habit and save almost nothing.

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The hairdresser keeps the chair, the advice and the teaching; client cards, aftercare notes and planning move into the salon system.
role.ambitious_version: A stylist with every client's history at the chair and assistants booked only for what they can do.
